client: I just feel so empty since Max passed away last month. Even simple things like going for walks in our favorite park just make me miss him more. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain just feels too deep.
therapist: "It sounds like the loss of Max has left a deep void, and even familiar places now feel heavy with his absence. When you say the pain feels too deep, can you tell me more about what that pain feels like to you?"

client: It’s like this constant ache in my chest, like something’s missing that will never come back. I feel guilty too—like maybe I didn’t do enough for him when he was here. I don’t know if talking about it will make that guilt go away or just make it worse.
therapist: "That ache and guilt sound like they’re carrying a heavy weight for you right now. It’s not uncommon to wonder if we could’ve done more, even when we’ve done our best. What do you think Max would say if he could hear those thoughts of guilt?"

client: I think Max would tell me not to blame myself—he was always so kind and forgiving. But it’s hard to believe that right now. I keep replaying moments when I feel like I could’ve been there more for him, and it’s haunting me. I’m not sure how to stop those thoughts from spiraling.
therapist: "It sounds like Max’s kindness is still present in your memories, even if it’s hard to fully embrace that reassurance right now. When those moments replay in your mind, what’s one small way you could gently redirect your focus to the love you shared, rather than the guilt?"

client: I guess I could try to think about the times we laughed together or the walks we shared, but it feels like those memories are overshadowed by the guilt right now. It’s hard to focus on the good when the regrets feel so loud. I’m not sure if I can just switch my focus like that.
therapist: "It sounds like the regrets are so present right now that they’re making it hard to fully connect with the warmth of those happier memories. When those regrets feel loud, what would it feel like to gently acknowledge them without letting them take over?"

client: I’m not sure how to acknowledge them without feeling overwhelmed. Every time I try to think about Max, the guilt just floods in and takes over. It feels like I’m stuck in this loop where I can’t escape the regret, no matter how hard I try.
therapist: "It sounds like the guilt feels so powerful right now that it’s hard to find any space for lighter memories or peace. When you’re stuck in that loop, would it feel possible to pause for a moment and ask yourself, ‘What would Max want me to feel right now?’"

client: Max would probably want me to remember the good times instead of dwelling on the guilt, but it’s easier said than done. When I try to pause and think about what he’d want, I still feel like I’m failing him somehow. It’s like I can’t let myself off the hook, even if he would.
therapist: "It sounds like Max’s kindness is still guiding you, even if it’s hard to fully accept that kindness for yourself right now. When you feel like you’re failing him, what would it look like to extend even a small bit of the same compassion to yourself that you know he would offer?"

client: I don’t know if I’m ready to be kind to myself about this—it feels like I’d be letting Max down if I stopped holding myself accountable. I know he’d want me to move forward, but it’s like I’m punishing myself for not being perfect when he needed me the most. It’s hard to imagine letting that go.
therapist: "It sounds like holding onto this accountability feels like a way to honor Max, even though it’s causing you pain. When you think about ‘letting go,’ what comes to mind? Is there a way to honor him that feels less like punishment and more like healing?"

client: Letting go feels like I’m betraying him somehow—like if I stop feeling guilty, I’ll forget how much he mattered. I don’t want to forget him, but I also don’t want to keep hurting like this. It’s hard to imagine a way to honor him that doesn’t involve holding onto this pain.
therapist: "It sounds like the guilt has become tangled with your love for Max, almost as if letting go of one might mean letting go of the other. What would it feel like to honor him by focusing on the ways he brought joy into your life, rather than the pain of what you feel you didn’t do?"

client: Focusing on the joy feels... complicated. I know Max brought so much light into my life, but it’s hard to separate that from the guilt about the times I feel I let him down. I’m scared that if I stop focusing on what I did wrong, I’ll lose touch with how much he meant to me. It’s like the guilt is keeping him close, in a way.
therapist: "It sounds like the guilt has become a way to stay connected to Max, almost like it’s a bridge to him in your grief. That’s a heavy bridge to carry, though—one that’s also keeping you from fully embracing the joy he brought. What would it feel like to imagine honoring him by building a different kind of bridge, one rooted in love and gratitude rather than guilt?"

client: Building a bridge rooted in love and gratitude sounds nice in theory, but it feels so far out of reach right now. I don’t know how to shift from guilt to gratitude when the guilt feels so ingrained. It’s like I’m stuck in this cycle, and I’m not sure how to start breaking free.
therapist: "It sounds like the guilt feels so familiar and deep-rooted that the idea of shifting to gratitude seems overwhelming right now. That’s okay—it’s not about forcing a change, but about taking small steps. What’s one small memory of Max that brings you warmth, even if the guilt tries to creep in?"
